title: Progressive overload
statement: Strength and size keep improving when training demand rises gradually over time: more reps at a load first, then more load, or more sets. A common guideline is a 2–10% load increase once you beat the target reps by 1–2.

sources.title: ACSM Position Stand: Progression models in resistance training for healthy adults

title: Volume and muscle growth
statement: More weekly sets per muscle generally build more muscle, with diminishing returns. In a meta-analysis, 10 or more weekly sets per muscle produced more growth than fewer than 5.

sources.title: Schoenfeld, Ogborn, Krieger. Dose-response relationship between weekly resistance training volume and increases in muscle mass

title: Weekly sets per muscle
statement: For most trained lifters about 10–20 hard sets per muscle per week is a productive range; beginners grow on less, and going far above your usual volume mostly adds fatigue.

sources.title: Baz-Valle et al. A systematic review of the effects of different resistance training volumes on muscle hypertrophy
Schoenfeld, Ogborn, Krieger. Dose-response relationship between weekly resistance training volume and increases in muscle mass

title: How close to failure
statement: Sets ending 0–3 reps short of failure build muscle well. Going to failure on every set adds fatigue and recovery time for little extra growth; keep it for the last set or isolation work.

sources.title: Refalo et al. Influence of resistance training proximity-to-failure on skeletal muscle hypertrophy: a systematic review with meta-analysis
Grgic et al. Effects of resistance training performed to repetition failure or non-failure on muscular strength and hypertrophy: a systematic review and meta-analysis

title: Rep ranges by goal
statement: Muscle grows across a wide range, roughly 6–30 reps, when sets are taken close to failure. Maximal strength improves most with heavier loads, about 1–6 reps, because strength is specific to heavy practice.

sources.title: Schoenfeld et al. Loading recommendations for muscle strength, hypertrophy, and local endurance: a re-examination of the repetition continuum
Schoenfeld et al. Strength and hypertrophy adaptations between low- vs. high-load resistance training

title: Rest between sets
statement: Resting about 2 minutes or more between sets of big compound lifts supports strength and muscle gain better than very short rests. 60–120 seconds is fine for isolation work.

sources.title: Schoenfeld et al. Longer interset rest periods enhance muscle strength and hypertrophy in resistance-trained men
Grgic et al. The effects of short versus long inter-set rest intervals in resistance training on measures of muscle hypertrophy: a systematic review

title: Training frequency
statement: With weekly volume equal, training a muscle 2 times a week is at least as good as once. Frequency mostly helps by spreading the same sets into better-quality sessions.

sources.title: Schoenfeld, Grgic, Krieger. How many times per week should a muscle be trained to maximize muscle hypertrophy?

title: Deload weeks
statement: A planned lighter week (fewer sets, lighter loads) helps shed accumulated fatigue. Practice commonly places one every 4–8 weeks for 5–7 days; direct evidence is limited and mostly expert consensus.

sources.title: Bell et al. Integrating deloading into strength and physique sports training programmes: an international Delphi consensus

title: Warming up
statement: A few progressively heavier warm-up sets improve performance on heavy lifts. Long static stretches right before lifting, over about 60 seconds per muscle, can briefly reduce strength; short ones are fine.

sources.title: Behm et al. Acute effects of muscle stretching on physical performance, range of motion, and injury incidence in healthy active individuals

title: Estimating a one-rep max
statement: A one-rep max can be estimated from a set: Epley uses load × (1 + reps / 30). Estimates are most accurate from sets of about 10 reps or fewer; above that they drift.

sources.title: LeSuer et al. The accuracy of prediction equations for estimating 1-RM performance in the bench press, squat, and deadlift

title: Plateaus
statement: Stalls are normal. Common fixes: change the rep range or the exercise variation, manage fatigue with a lighter week, check sleep and protein, and progress in smaller steps. Evidence is mostly practical experience.

sources.title: Kraemer, Ratamess. Fundamentals of resistance training: progression and exercise prescription

title: Time off and coming back
statement: Strength holds up well for about 3 weeks without training, and muscle lost over longer breaks comes back faster on retraining than it took to build the first time.

sources.title: Bosquet et al. Effect of training cessation on muscular performance: a meta-analysis

title: How long recovery takes
statement: Muscle performance after hard lifting usually recovers within 24–72 hours. Sessions taken to failure, with lots of lowering work or heavy compound lifts, sit at the longer end.

sources.title: Morán-Navarro et al. Time course of recovery following resistance training leading or not to failure

title: Muscle soreness (DOMS)
statement: Soreness after unfamiliar training peaks around 24–72 hours and fades with repeated exposure. It is a poor sign of how much a session built muscle.

sources.title: Cheung, Hume, Maxwell. Delayed onset muscle soreness: treatment strategies and performance factors

title: Sleep and training
statement: Short or poor sleep lowers strength endurance, mood and motivation, and slows recovery. A single bad night hurts repeated efforts more than one maximal lift.

sources.title: Craven et al. Effects of acute sleep loss on physical performance: a systematic and meta-analytic review

title: How much sleep
statement: Adults should regularly sleep 7 or more hours a night for health; many athletes benefit from more.

sources.title: Watson et al. Recommended amount of sleep for a healthy adult: AASM and SRS joint consensus

title: Daily protein
statement: For people lifting to build muscle, about 1.6 g of protein per kg of body weight a day captures most of the benefit; up to 2.2 g/kg is a reasonable upper target.

sources.title: Morton et al. A systematic review, meta-analysis and meta-regression of the effect of protein supplementation on resistance training-induced gains
Jäger et al. ISSN Position Stand: protein and exercise

title: Spreading protein
statement: Total daily protein matters most. Splitting it into 3–5 meals of about 0.4 g/kg each is a sensible way to reach it; the post-workout window is wide.

sources.title: Schoenfeld, Aragon. How much protein can the body use in a single meal for muscle-building?
Jäger et al. ISSN Position Stand: protein and exercise

title: Keeping muscle while dieting
statement: In a calorie deficit, keep lifting and eat more protein, around 1.6–2.4 g/kg a day, to hold on to muscle. Slower loss helps too.

sources.title: Helms et al. A systematic review of dietary protein during caloric restriction in resistance trained lean athletes
Hector, Phillips. Protein recommendations for weight loss in elite athletes

title: Rate of weight change
statement: Losing about 0.5–1% of body weight a week preserves muscle and strength better than faster loss for lean lifters. For gaining, about 0.25–0.5% a week limits fat gain.

sources.title: Garthe et al. Effect of two different weight-loss rates on body composition and strength and power-related performance in elite athletes
Iraki et al. Nutrition recommendations for bodybuilders in the off-season

title: Creatine
statement: Creatine monohydrate, 3–5 g a day, safely adds to strength and lean mass gains from training in most people. Loading is optional.

sources.title: Kreider et al. ISSN position stand: safety and efficacy of creatine supplementation in exercise, sport, and medicine

title: Caffeine
statement: Caffeine at 3–6 mg per kg of body weight, about 60 minutes before training, modestly improves performance. Late doses can cost sleep.

sources.title: Guest et al. ISSN position stand: caffeine and exercise performance

title: Hydration
statement: Losing more than about 2% of body weight through sweat can impair performance. Drinking to thirst works for most sessions; weigh before and after long ones.

sources.title: Sawka et al. ACSM position stand: exercise and fluid replacement

title: What BMI can't tell you
statement: BMI is weight for height: 18.5–24.9 is 'normal', 25 overweight, 30 obese. It cannot tell muscle from fat, so muscular people often read as overweight.

sources.title: WHO. Obesity: preventing and managing the global epidemic
Rothman. BMI-related errors in the measurement of obesity

title: Tape-measure body fat
statement: The US Navy tape method estimates body fat typically within about 3–4 percentage points of lab methods. Use it for your trend, measured the same way each time.

sources.title: Hodgdon, Beckett. Prediction of percent body fat for U.S. Navy men and women from body circumferences and height

title: Resting heart rate
statement: Adult resting heart rate is usually 60–100 bpm, lower in trained people. A rise of several beats above your own baseline can signal fatigue, illness, stress or poor sleep.

sources.title: Buchheit. Monitoring training status with HR measures: do all roads lead to Rome?

title: Heart-rate variability
statement: HRV is useful against your own baseline, not other people's. Daily readings are noisy, so a 7-day rolling average tracks recovery better than one morning.

sources.title: Plews et al. Training adaptation and heart rate variability in elite endurance athletes
Buchheit. Monitoring training status with HR measures

title: Heart-rate zones
statement: Zones based on heart-rate reserve (max minus resting) fit individuals better than % of max alone. Max heart rate can be estimated as 208 − 0.7 × age.

sources.title: Tanaka, Monahan, Seals. Age-predicted maximal heart rate revisited

title: Resting by heart rate
statement: Resting until heart rate drops back toward a set level is a practical way to fit rest to the person and the set. Direct evidence in lifting is limited.

sources.title: Buchheit. Monitoring training status with HR measures

title: Lifting after 50 and 60
statement: Older adults gain strength and muscle from resistance training at any age. 2–3 sessions a week work well; recovery can take a little longer, so progress steadily.

sources.title: Fragala et al. Resistance training for older adults: position statement from the NSCA

title: Starting out
statement: Beginners progress quickly on modest volume: 2–3 full-body sessions a week with a few sets per exercise is enough. Technique first, then add load.

sources.title: ACSM Position Stand: Progression models in resistance training for healthy adults

title: Training under 18
statement: Supervised resistance training is safe and useful for young people. Focus on technique and gradual progress; avoid maximal lifts without a qualified coach.

sources.title: Lloyd et al. Position statement on youth resistance training: the 2014 International Consensus

title: Pain red flags
statement: Stop the movement and see a physio or doctor for pain that is sharp, spreading, numb or tingling, wakes you at night, or comes with swelling.

sources.title: Finucane et al. International framework for red flags for potential serious spinal pathologies

title: Tendons and load
statement: Tendons adapt more slowly than muscle. Gradual increases and heavy, slow reps help them; sudden spikes in load or volume raise the risk of irritation.

sources.title: Magnusson, Kjaer. The impact of loading, unloading, ageing and injury on the human tendon
Beyer et al. Heavy slow resistance versus eccentric training as treatment for Achilles tendinopathy

title: Cardio and lifting
statement: Cardio alongside lifting barely affects muscle growth. High running volume close to lifting can blunt some strength and power gains; separating them or favouring cycling helps.

sources.title: Schumann et al. Compatibility of concurrent aerobic and strength training for skeletal muscle size and function: an updated systematic review and meta-analysis

title: Daily steps
statement: More daily steps lower mortality risk, levelling off around 6,000–8,000 a day for adults over 60 and 8,000–10,000 for younger adults.

sources.title: Paluch et al. Daily steps and all-cause mortality: a meta-analysis of 15 international cohorts

title: Alcohol and recovery
statement: Heavy drinking after training lowered muscle protein synthesis in a lab study, by about 24% even with protein and 37% without. Occasional moderate drinks matter far less.

sources.title: Parr et al. Alcohol ingestion impairs maximal post-exercise rates of myofibrillar protein synthesis

title: Life stress
statement: High ongoing psychological stress slowed recovery of muscle function over the 96 hours after a hard session in one study. On stressful weeks, keep sessions shorter or lighter.

sources.title: Stults-Kolehmainen et al. Chronic psychological stress impairs recovery of muscular function and somatic sensations over a 96-hour period

title: Menstrual cycle and training
statement: Evidence that cycle phase meaningfully changes strength or muscle gain is weak and inconsistent. Adjust by how you feel rather than a fixed phase plan.

sources.title: McNulty et al. The effects of menstrual cycle phase on exercise performance in eumenorrheic women: a systematic review and meta-analysis
Colenso-Semple et al. Current evidence shows no influence of women's menstrual cycle phase on acute strength performance or adaptations to resistance exercise training

title: Stretching and mobility
statement: Stretching improves range of motion but does not prevent soreness. Lifting through a full range improves flexibility about as well as stretching does.

sources.title: Afonso et al. The effectiveness of resistance training versus stretching on flexibility: a systematic review and meta-analysis
Herbert et al. Stretching to prevent or reduce muscle soreness after exercise (Cochrane)

title: Coaching cues
statement: Cues that point attention outward ('push the floor away') often produce more force and better movement than cues about body parts ('squeeze your glutes').

sources.title: Wulf. Attentional focus and motor learning: a review of 15 years

title: Plates, bars and units
statement: Standard plates are 25, 20, 15, 10, 5, 2.5 and 1.25 kg or 45, 35, 25, 10, 5 and 2.5 lb. An Olympic bar is 20 kg; a common US bar is 45 lb (20.4 kg). A dumbbell rack's step decides your next loadable jump.

sources.title: IWF Technical and Competition Rules and Regulations

title: Estimating calorie needs
statement: Daily energy needs are resting metabolism times activity. Mifflin-St Jeor is the most accurate common resting equation, within about 10% for most adults; adjust from your weight trend.

sources.title: Frankenfield, Roth-Yousey, Compher. Comparison of predictive equations for resting metabolic rate in healthy nonobese and obese adults

title: Rating effort (reps in reserve)
statement: Guesses of reps left are accurate to about 1 rep close to failure and get worse further from it; they improve with practice. Rate every set and the app learns your bias.

sources.title: Halperin et al. Accuracy in predicting repetitions to task failure in resistance exercise: a scoping review and exploratory meta-analysis
Zourdos et al. Novel resistance training-specific RPE scale measuring repetitions in reserve

title: Choosing exercises
statement: Compound and isolation exercises both build muscle. Compounds are efficient; isolation fills gaps. Varying angles over time develops a muscle more completely.

sources.title: Gentil et al. Single vs. multi-joint resistance exercises: effects on muscle strength and hypertrophy

title: Range of motion
statement: Full range, and especially work at long muscle lengths, tends to build as much or more muscle than short partial reps.

sources.title: Pallarés et al. Effects of range of motion on resistance training adaptations: a systematic review and meta-analysis

title: Session length
statement: Session length follows how many sets you do and how long you rest between them. Guidance for strength and muscle gain is given as sets, loads and rest, not as minutes per session; heavy sets get the longest rests.

sources.title: ACSM Position Stand: Progression models in resistance training for healthy adults
